title: Pauline Hanson adds to confusion over One Nation’s immigration policy – as it happened
text:
One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has said the party’s net migration policy remains at 130,000 but would include Pacific labour workers on top in comments that seemingly confirm those made by David Farley earlier this week.
Speaking on a panel at News Corp’s Bush Summit this afternoon, Hanson was asked if that meant more than 130,000 visa holders each year.
Hanson: “Correct, because your Palm [Pacific Australia Labour Mobility] workers, rural and regional Australia would die if they didn’t have the workers coming in, and especially the abattoirs and the farmers. So that’s a different program. These people are given accommodation by the farming sector and the businesses that employ them. So that is not the big impact here. But with immigration, you can’t just tie it to your housing, because infrastructure is another big thing and hospitals and schools and the nursing homes – that has to be all accounted for so it’s just not about houses.”
Moderator: “So was David Farley wrong or right this week?”
Hanson: “David Farley, he didn’t understand, he got confused about the visa holders because he went on to say Palm workers, as I’ve always said. Palm workers is the visa-holders that can come into the country. They’re provided accommodation, usually by those on the farms. They’re not taking up the housing. So that’s a totally different matter.”
On Sunday, Farley told ABC’s Insiders that One Nation’s net overseas migration (Nom) target was 130,000 plus an additional 100,000 Palm and skilled workers, and backpackers.
That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage after a jam-packed news day.
Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:
At least 34 Australian tourists are reportedly missing in the deadly flash floods that swept through the Nepal-Tibet border. Fourteen of them missing in Himalayas are members of same religious group.
The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has defended national cabinet’s decision to drop strict mandates requiring new AI datacentres to be powered entirely by renewable energy.
The former Treasury secretary Ken Henry says the GST deal benefiting Western Australia is “stupid” and undermines the “integrity of the system of horizontal fiscal equalisation”.
The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced he will scrap a levy on public transport users the government secretly introduced to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop.
Unexpectedly strong inflation figures have forced a rethink on interest rates, with three out of four big banks now tipping the RBA to hike rates again by Melbourne Cup day.
One person has died and two others are in hospital after a “serious traffic incident” in Canberra reportedly involving three cyclists and a car.
Two men from Western Australia have been charged as part of an alleged cybercrime syndicate authorities say created malicious software to rob thousands of businesses around the globe.
Household spending has grown at fastest rate since mid-2023, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
A pro-Israel activist has been ordered to pay costs after the federal court found he breached parts of a legal settlement with Sydney restaurant Cairo Takeaway.
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has added to the confusion on the the party’s net migration policy.
Jean Nassif, the property developer who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022 after his company Toplace collapsed, will appear by video link to give evidence to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption next Friday.
Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.
Parramatta Powerhouse CEO steps aside 72 days before opening amid procurement investigation
The chief executive of the Powerhouse Parramatta, Lisa Havilah, has stood aside 72 days before the $915 museum opens to the public amid an investigation into procurement for the project.
Havilah, the inaugural CEO of the Powerhouse, has been in the role since 2019. In a message to Powerhouse staff this afternoon, the secretary of the NSW Department of Creative Industries, Tourism, Hospitality and Sport (DCITHS), Melanie Hawyes, wrote that Havilah would stand aside amid an “an ongoing investigation into matters relating to governance and procurement practices at the Powerhouse”.
After speaking with the Chief Executive earlier today, Lisa Havilah will be standing aside while the investigation is completed.

I recognise that this news comes at a significant time for the organisation, as we prepare for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta. I know how much work, commitment and personal energy all of you have invested in reaching this milestone, and I want to assure you that there will be no impact to the existing programs of work, or the opening on 7 November.
The NSW government architect, Abbie Galvin, will take over as interim CEO, while former Sydney Opera House CEO, Louise Herron, who finished in that role this month, will provide “strategic advice and support”.
In a media release this afternoon, the NSW arts minister, John Graham, confirmed the “interim arrangements”.
I would like to thank the Powerhouse team for getting us to this point in the delivery of the Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest and most complex cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.
Jean Nassif, the property developer who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022 after his company Toplace collapsed, will appear by video link in the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption next Friday.
The fugitive developer is at the centre of an inquiry which is looking into whether Nassif made a $2m payment to a group of Liberal-aligned operatives known as the Reformers in order to secure certain political outcomes, including the removal of the then-building commissioner, David Chandler.
The Sydney construction and property development group Toplace collapsed into voluntary administration in July 2023, leaving behind more than $600m in debts, stalled projects, and apartment owners facing massive repair bills for serious building defects.
His daughter, Ashlyn Nassif, a lawyer, pleaded guilty to fraud charges in June.
Charles Perrottet, the former premier Dominic Perrottet’s brother, is due to appear tomorrow and for the early part of next week.
Fourteen Australians missing in Nepal who travelled to the region with the Himalayan Glacier tour group were part of the Hindu religious organisation Australia Bharatha Brahman Samajam, its co-founder, Vasan Srinivasan, said.
It’s a group with family connections. They are great contributors to our community and have assisted me with lots of my fundraising activities for mental health in New South Wales. They are all from around Sydney.
Srinivasan, who is also the chief executive officer of the Mental Health Foundation Australia, said he was using all of his contacts in government to find out their whereabouts.
Hopefully God can give me the privilege of getting them home to Sydney.
Queensland attorney general denies bill would eliminate independence of child oversight body
Continued from our previous post …
Deb Frecklington denied the new body would cease to be independent, in a Thursday afternoon press conference.
Frecklington said:
The commissioner, it is important to note, has independence for the regulatory functions of that commission.
So for example, if the commissioner of the day of the new protection commission determines to not grant a blue card or to grant a blue card, then I have no ability to interfere in that decision
Asked whether her power to hire and fire would mean that she could simply sack a commissioner for using those powers in a way she didn’t like, Frecklington rejected the premise of the question.
Former deputy commissioner Natalie Lewis said the new bill would hand control of the commission’s budget and staff to a department chief executive – the very sector the office exists to scrutinise. She said:
The Bill removes the Commissioner’s protection from removal, keeps the government’s power to direct the one function that matters most, and strips the office of its independent budget. You cannot call that stronger oversight. You can only call it oversight that answers to the very government it is meant to check.
Queensland attorney general tables bill giving herself power to hire, fire and direct state’s child safety oversight body
Queensland’s attorney general has tabled a bill that would give her the power to hire, fire and direct the state’s independent child safety oversight body.
The new bill establishes a new organisation, known as the Queensland Protection Commission, which would swallow the Queensland Family and Child Commission, a statutory body established in 2014 to oversee the state’s child safety system.
Deb Frecklington’s legislation would also remove a requirement for government to appoint at least one Indigenous commissioner. It could now be filled by a non-Indigenous person with “demonstrated ability or experience in working with Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children”.
About half the Queensland children in out of home care are Indigenous.
Under the bill, Frecklington will also have the power to hire or fire the commissioner “for any reason or none”, with signoff from the governor.
The commissioner is also subject to the direction of the minister and “must comply” with a direction.
The body will be responsible for both child safeguarding roles such as administrating the state’s working with children check system, coordinating with other bodies and law enforcement, and systemic oversight of the child protection system.
For Australians wondering how they can help those affected in the devastating Nepal flash floods, Unicef has launched an international emergency appeal on their website.

Unicef sends funds to assist in emergency health care, life-saving nutrition, safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene supplies, temporary shelter and child protection and psychosocial support.

A pro-Israel activist has been ordered to pay costs after the federal court found he breached parts of a legal settlement with Sydney restaurant Cairo Takeaway.
On Thursday, Justice Robert Bromwich ordered Ofir Birenbaum pay costs to the restaurant after the federal court found in June that he had breached the pair’s legal settlement after he and his lawyer, Rebekah Giles, released “highly misleading and even deceptive” statements that implied they had won.
Bromwich said in his reasons for awarding costs on Thursday:
The need for the respondents to seek declaratory relief was entirely driven by inappropriate conduct by Mr Birenbaum in relation to the Deed, both by him in person and on his behalf by his solicitor, Ms Giles …
That was made worse by the dismissive approach taken to the offers made by the respondents as to remedying that behaviour, and by the refusal to engage on the question of costs for reasons that I regard as largely spurious.
The decision ends the long-running feud involving Birenbaum, who visited the popular Middle Eastern restaurant wearing a Star of David cap and necklace, with reporters from the Daily Telegraph in February 2025.
The operation, later revealed to have been dubbed “undercover Jew” internally by the newspaper, made international headlines after it backfired.
In August, Birenbaum launched defamation proceedings against the restaurant’s owner, Hesham El Masry, and staff member Talaat Yehia for statements made in a series of social media posts.
The case reached a confidential settlement in March, which Bromwich found in June Birenbaum breached.
The settlement had involved Cairo Takeaway, Birenbaum and the Daily Telegraph releasing a joint statement in which the Daily Telegraph apologised to Cairo Takeaway for “causing distress”. Cairo apologised unreservedly to Birenbaum.
A map of the region affected by the flash flood in Nepal
More than 1,000 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet after a flash flood, with rescuers searching for hundreds of foreign tourists. Follow the latest on our live blog.
“Australians might be telling pollsters they’re doing it tough, but their credit cards clearly haven’t got the memo.”
That quote from an investment strategist neatly sums up figures from this morning which show we are in the midst of a surprising and counterintuitive boom in household spending.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics showed spending jumped by 1.1% in the month of July (nearly four times as fast as expected), which brought the annual growth rate to 7% – the fastest pace in more than three years.
The ABS’s monthly release pulls together de-identified card transactions, supermarket scanner data and motor vehicle sales figures.
It’s not just we’re being forced to fork out more on groceries and petrol: spending on non-essentials was up an even bigger 7.8% in the year to July as we splurged on clothing and footwear and attended sporting and cultural events.
This is all while consumer confidence is in the dumps and real wages go backwards.
Part of the increase in spending is explained by higher prices, but Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, admits it’s hard to explain.
“It is challenging to unpack, because we are getting mixed signals from a number of different sources,” Allen says.
She suspects some of the spending strength in July could be some payback from the initial caution that greeted the start of the Middle East conflict.
Maybe Australians are dipping into their savings to spend, and older households have been largely immune to higher interest rates and rents.
Whatever explains it, resilient spending adds to bets the Reserve Bank will need to do more to slow the economy if it wants to get inflation back to target.
Two men from Western Australia have been charged as part of an alleged cybercrime syndicate authorities say created malicious software to rob thousands of businesses around the globe.
The Australian federal police, WA police and the US FBI said in a joint release the men were charged with a combined 14 offences. Police will allege they were part of a “highly organised syndicate” that involved “large-scale cybercrime offending, including data intrusion, identity crime, and cryptocurrency-based money laundering”.
Police will allege the syndicate inserted malicious code into software on an open-source platform, which was then used unwittingly by other developers. That infected software was then distributed to computer systems across governments, academia and the private sector which allegedly allowed the syndicate to harvest or steal data.
Police allege the code compromised more than 1,000 organisations and enabled the theft of more than 500,000 credentials. The financial impact is expected to be hundreds of millions of dollars in global remediation costs.
The men, aged 21 and 23, are scheduled to appear in court today.
Glacial collapse caused huge flood leaving hundreds dead or missing in Nepal and Tibet
A glacial collapse triggered the catastrophic flash flood in Nepal and Tibet that roared down valleys, wiping out entire villages and leaving a preliminary death toll of at least 165 people, the US Geological Survey said. Rescuers on Thursday raced to locate the hundreds missing, including nationals from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
Early reports from Nepali ​officials initially suggested an earthquake in the area could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4 magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred.”
An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated that a landslide of ice and rock triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 20km north-east of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s national disaster authority said. Experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas.

Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama dies aged 97
Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97.
Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her studio announced in a statement on her website on Thursday.
“Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read.
She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.
